passage: Historians have lately read the medieval bill of exchange as disguised lending: a bill bought in Florence at one rate and paid in Bruges at another yielded a return, and lending at interest was forbidden by the Church. But the surviving letters between branches of the Florentine banking houses are about roads. They report which passes a lord had closed, which convoys had been taken, and what a guard cost by the mile, and where a bill went unpaid the loss the writers count is the coin they would otherwise have sent. The gap between the two rates, when the letters mention it at all, is treated as the fee for a service, known in advance and often smaller than the guard it replaced. The ban on usury, which the letters nowhere mention, belongs to the theologians who wrote about the bill afterward. For the men who used it, the bill was a ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The letters are taken up with danger on the roads, and when a bill fails the loss they reckon is the coin that would otherwise have travelled, so for its users the bill was a guard against loss in transit: a *precaution*. *evasion* is ruled out by "The ban on usury, which the letters nowhere mention, belongs to the theologians who wrote about the bill afterward": the men using the bill were not working around a prohibition they never had in mind. *speculation* is ruled out by "known in advance and often smaller than the guard it replaced"; a fixed, modest fee is not a gamble on the rate. *formality* is ruled out by "which passes a lord had closed, which convoys had been taken, and what a guard cost by the mile": the danger the bill answered was real and priced, so the instrument was no empty procedure.

passage: Milestones along the Roman roads name the emperor under whom they were set up, and they were long read as a record of construction: count the stones of one reign and you have that reign's road building. But many stones stand beside roads that had been paved centuries earlier, the surfaces near them show no resurfacing of that date, and some carry the names of two or three emperors cut in succession, each new name chiselled over the last and set in the same builder's formula, as though the newcomer had laid the road himself. The stones were not marking new roads. They were ______ old ones, in the name of whoever happened to rule.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The stones put the current emperor's name on roads he had not built and cut it over the names of his predecessors, so each ruler was asserting ownership of existing roads: *claiming* them. *repairing* is ruled out by "the surfaces near them show no resurfacing of that date": nothing was done to the road itself. *extending* is ruled out by "roads that had been paved centuries earlier" and by the last sentence's "old ones"; no new length was added. *commemorating* is ruled out by "set in the same builder's formula, as though the newcomer had laid the road himself": the inscription credits the reigning emperor with the road rather than honouring whoever built it, and "each new name chiselled over the last" shows the earlier emperors erased, not remembered.

passage: Novels issued in monthly parts end each instalment on suspended action, and critics now read the device as architecture: the break fell where the author wanted the reader held. The authors' own papers are less flattering. Revising for publication in volumes, when the monthly number no longer had to sell, the same writers ran parts together and smoothed the joins, so that a chapter that had ended on a fall from a horse now ended with the rider safely home. One of them asks his publisher whether "the usual precipice" might be spared from a quiet number and is told it may not, and the same letter discusses where a scene should end in quite different terms. For these writers the suspended ending was a matter of ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The writers dropped the breaks as soon as the monthly sale no longer required them, and one who asked to leave a break out was refused, so the suspended ending was something demanded of them: a matter of *obligation*. *design* is ruled out by "the same writers ran parts together and smoothed the joins": an author who removes the device the moment he is free of it did not build his book around it. *habit* is ruled out by "asks his publisher whether 'the usual precipice' might be spared"; a writer asking leave to omit the break is not producing it unthinkingly, and it was kept because he "is told it may not." *chance* is ruled out by the same request: a break called "the usual precipice" and negotiated in advance with a publisher does not fall where it happens to fall.

passage: The settling of English spelling in the sixteenth century is now usually credited to the printing houses: compositors, setting the same words thousands of times, are said to have kept whichever forms filled a line of type conveniently and dropped the rest. The printed books are against this. In the output of the largest houses a word is spelled two ways on a single page, lengthened or shortened to make the line come out even, and the practice continues into the 1640s, sixty years after the schoolmasters' tables of correct forms began to appear. The forms that finally became fixed are the ones in those tables, chosen there to display a word's derivation, and many of them are longer than the forms the compositors had favoured; where a table and a printing house disagreed, it was the printing house that gave way. Standard spelling was a(n) ______ of the schoolroom, and it reached the printing house late and from outside.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The fixed forms are the ones the schoolmasters' tables laid down, and the printers adopted them a generation later, so standard spelling was something the schoolroom made: an *invention* of the schoolroom. *convenience* is ruled out by "many of them are longer than the forms the compositors had favoured" and by "chosen there to display a word's derivation": the winning forms were picked for their etymology, not their fit in a line. *accident* is ruled out by "the schoolmasters' tables of correct forms"; forms laid out in a table of what is correct are deliberate. *concession* is ruled out by "where a table and a printing house disagreed, it was the printing house that gave way": the schoolroom yielded nothing.

passage: The hallmarks struck into medieval silver have lately been read as a guild's weapon against outsiders: by controlling the mark, the argument runs, the town's smiths kept foreign work off their market. The assay records do not bear this out. Imported pieces were brought to the assay like any others, and those that reached the standard were marked and sold; what the wardens refused was metal below the standard, whoever had worked it. Silver could not lawfully be sold without the mark, the fines for selling it unmarked were paid over to the buyer, doubled, and the smiths prosecuted most often were the guild's own members. The mark itself was struck on the underside of a piece, where no one admiring it would see. On the records' evidence, the mark's purpose was ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The wardens refused only substandard metal, the fines went doubled to the buyer who had been cheated, and the guild prosecuted its own members, so the mark served the person buying the silver: its purpose was *protective*. *exclusionary* is ruled out by "Imported pieces were brought to the assay like any others, and those that reached the standard were marked and sold": foreign work of good metal was let in. *advisory* is ruled out by "Silver could not lawfully be sold without the mark"; the mark was compulsory, not guidance. *decorative* is ruled out by "struck on the underside of a piece, where no one admiring it would see".

passage: Eighteenth-century treatises complain that singers smothered arias in ornaments the composer never wrote, and modern editions strip such ornaments away in order to recover what the composer meant. But composers' own manuscripts write out the first section of an aria in detail and leave its repeat almost bare on the page, and letters from composers to their singers ask for particular embellishments by name. Far from recording the composer's intention, the bare repeat was his ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A repeat left bare by a composer who, in his letters, asks singers for specific embellishments is a space he meant them to fill: an *invitation*. *oversight* is ruled out by the contrast with the first section, which the same manuscripts "write out ... in detail"; a composer who takes that care has not forgotten the repeat. *compromise* would mean the composer yielded ornaments to singers against his wishes, but the letters "ask for particular embellishments by name." *rebuke* is ruled out by the same letters: a composer who requests ornaments is not reproaching singers for adding them.

passage: English took its words for cooked meat—beef, pork, mutton—from French while keeping native words for the living animals, and the split is taught as a snapshot of the Norman Conquest: French-speaking lords ate what English-speaking peasants raised. The earliest citations tell a slower story. For two centuries after the Conquest the French words appear only in texts written in French, and when "beef" finally enters English it names the animal as well as the meat, narrowing to the table only later, in the mouths of speakers who had no lords to please. The pairing that seems to record a social division at a single moment was in fact ______ over generations.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The division of labour between the French and English words emerged gradually, long after the Conquest and among ordinary speakers, so it was *settled* over generations. *imposed* is ruled out by "appear only in texts written in French" for two centuries and by "speakers who had no lords to please": no one was in a position to dictate the split, and it arrived too late to be a Conquest-era decree. *resisted* is ruled out by "names the animal as well as the meat, narrowing to the table only later": the word was taken up and its meaning drifted into the pairing, which is an outcome speakers arrived at, not one they fought. *forgotten* contradicts the first sentence, which shows the pairing still in use and being taught.

passage: Mining companies that paid wages in scrip redeemable only at the company store are remembered for the store's prices, and the scrip is described as a device for keeping workers in debt. Account books from several such towns show something less dramatic. Most families ended the month with a small credit, and store prices ran only a little above those in the nearest town. What the scrip prevented was not solvency but ______. A worker with a month's wages in company paper could not buy a train ticket, and the company knew it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The sentence after the blank supplies the mechanism: scrip could not buy "a train ticket," so what it prevented was leaving, or *departure*. *saving* is ruled out by "Most families ended the month with a small credit"; families did put money by. *credit* is a trap set by that same sentence, which shows workers holding credit, not being denied it; the passage also says the debt story is "less dramatic" than remembered. *comparison* is ruled out by "store prices ran only a little above those in the nearest town": the passage itself makes the comparison and finds little in it, so hiding prices was not what the scrip achieved.

passage: Marble copies made in Roman workshops after Greek bronzes carry tree stumps and struts that the originals did not need, and the additions are usually dismissed as supports the marble required. Yet copies from one workshop show the same pose with a strut in one version and without it in another, though the block is the same stone, and on several copies the figure is summary work while the strut beside it is finished with care, its bark cut leaf by leaf. Buyers, it seems, wanted the strut. A stump beside the ankle told a visitor that the statue reproduced a famous bronze, and the copy's value lay in its ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The stump's job was to announce that the statue descended from a famous original, so what buyers paid for was the copy's *pedigree*. *material* is ruled out by "though the block is the same stone": the marble was identical with and without the feature buyers wanted. *workmanship* is ruled out by "the figure is summary work while the strut beside it is finished with care": buyers accepted rough carving on the statue itself, so skill was not what they were paying for. *pose* is ruled out by "the same pose with a strut in one version and without it in another": the pose stayed constant while the feature that carried the value came and went.

passage: A fugitive who reached a medieval English church could claim sanctuary, and the custom is usually described as mercy: the church placed itself between a criminal and the gallows. But one coroner's rolls show that nearly every sanctuary-seeker was made to confess the crime before the coroner, to forfeit his goods to the crown, and to leave the kingdom within forty days by a road he was forbidden to stray from. For the crown this was a conviction obtained without a trial. Sanctuary was less a(n) ______ than a procedure, and the church's part in it was to supply the room.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The passage sets up the view that sanctuary spared the criminal and then shows it delivering confession, forfeiture and exile on a fixed timetable, so it was less a *reprieve* than a procedure. *punishment* fails because the passage shows sanctuary WAS punishing: "to forfeit his goods to the crown, and to leave the kingdom"; saying it was "less a punishment" contradicts that sentence. *negotiation* is ruled out by "was made to confess the crime before the coroner, to forfeit his goods to the crown, and to leave the kingdom within forty days by a road he was forbidden to stray from": every term was dictated and nothing was bargained. *ceremony* is ruled out by "For the crown this was a conviction obtained without a trial": the arrangement had legal effect, so it was not an empty rite.

passage: The tolls charged on eighteenth-century English canals were fixed by Parliament in each canal's founding act, which set both a ceiling and a floor: a company could charge no more than the published schedule, and could not carry one merchant's coal for less than it charged another for the same cargo. Historians have lately made the floor the traders' device, a guarantee that no rival would be given a better rate. The petitions tell it the other way. Those asking for the floors came from the companies, whose shareholders wanted an end to rate-cutting between rival canals. The traders' petitions do not mention the floor at all; they ask that the maxima be cut, and they complain of each revision of the act since, for a rate stood where the act had put it until Parliament moved it, and Parliament had moved it upward every time. What the traders feared was ______ tolls.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The traders asked for lower maxima and objected to every revision of the act, each of which had moved the schedule upward, so what they feared was the rate going up: *rising* tolls. *unequal* is the reading the second sentence attributes to historians and is ruled out by "Those asking for the floors came from the companies" and "The traders' petitions do not mention the floor at all": the rule against one merchant paying less than another was not the traders' concern. *hidden* is ruled out by "fixed by Parliament in each canal's founding act" and "the published schedule"; the rates were public. *discretionary* is ruled out by "a rate stood where the act had put it until Parliament moved it": no company could alter a toll at its own discretion, so what the traders objected to was the direction of lawful change, not a company setting rates as it pleased.

passage: The chapter headings of eighteenth-century comic novels announce the events to come—"In which our hero is robbed"—and modern readers find them clumsy, as though the author could not resist giving away his own story. But these novels were read aloud in households over many evenings, and the person reading, by the custom of the time, passed over the heading and began with the chapter. The headings were gathered instead in a table of contents at the front, where a listener who had missed a night could find the place at which to rejoin, and they stand over the grave chapters as evenly as over the comic ones. For those households the heading was a(n) ______, and what looks clumsy now is only the distance from that room.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The headings let "a listener who had missed a night" locate "the place at which to rejoin," so they marked a position in the book: a *bookmark*. *preview* is ruled out by "the person reading, by the custom of the time, passed over the heading and began with the chapter": the listeners never heard a heading ahead of its events. *confession* takes up "could not resist giving away," but that is the modern misreading, and "gathered instead in a table of contents at the front" shows a deliberate apparatus, not an author letting something slip. *joke* is ruled out by "they stand over the grave chapters as evenly as over the comic ones".

passage: Long runs of grain prices are the economic historian's thermometer for the pre-industrial harvest: a bad year shows as a spike. But prices were recorded at markets, and in the worst years the markets of remote districts recorded nothing at all, because no grain came in to be sold. The series that survive unbroken belong to towns able to draw grain from a distance. Those towns felt the shortage, and their prices rose; but they felt it at one remove, and the rise was smaller than the empty markets' would have been. The worst famines are therefore ______ in the record, precisely because they were the worst.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The only complete series come from towns where "the rise was smaller than the empty markets' would have been," so the surviving record makes the worst famines look milder than they were: *muted*. *exaggerated* is ruled out by "recorded nothing at all" and by "the rise was smaller"; the bias runs the other way. *undetectable* is ruled out by "Those towns felt the shortage, and their prices rose": the famine appears in the record, only softened. *delayed* has no support; the passage describes missing entries and dampened spikes, not late ones.
